description.narrative:
ICTJs 5-year strategic plan is designed around one main objective: Societies implement transitional justice solutions to address legacies of massive human rights violations and lay the foundations for peace, justice, and inclusion.
The two global outcomes that will contribute to reaching the overall objective are:
1) Societies implement responsive and gender-sensitive solutions to address the legacies of massive human rights violations.
2) Practitioners and policymakers at the international level have better information and expanded capacity to advance responsive, gender-sensitive, and context-specific solutions.
This reflects ICTJs two major arenas of implementation country-specific interventions and global policy work aiming to shape global transitional justice knowledge and practice.
With this contribution, Sida will support the first four years of the 5-year strategic plan. The summary of the strategic plan includes some targets for different stages of the agreement period (Dox 012597/22) and thus constitutes relevant input to what is expected to be achieved by the end of the contribution.

Detta bidrag är en förnyad fas av kärnstöd till den internationella organisationen International Centre for Transitional Justice (ICTJ) under en period på fyra år och med ett totalt belopp på 40 MSEK.
ICTJ är en nyckelaktör inom området övergångsrättvisa (TJ) och är både en expertorganisation, en aktör inom policyutveckling och en partner till det civila samhället, offentliga institutioner och regeringar på landnivå. ICTJ genomför långsiktiga och omfattande program i ett antal länder men svarar också på förfrågningar om ad hoc-engagemang i ytterligare sammanhang när det anses relevant. ICTJ har sitt huvudkontor i New York och kontor i Bryssel, Haag, Colombia, Libanon, Gambia, Tunisien och Uganda.
ICTJ arbetar för att samhällen skall hantera massiva brott mot mänskliga rättigheter på ett ansvarsfullt, genderkänsligt och kontextanpassat sätt, samt för att yrkesverksamma och beslutsfattare på internationell nivå har bättre information och utökad kapacitet att främja sådana lösningar. Detta förväntas i sin tur bidra till att undvika återfall i våldsam konflikt samt främja hållbar fred.
Den totala budgeten för ICTJ:s verksamhet för de fyra åren är cirka 442 miljoner SEK. Andra bidrag kommer från institutionella givare, varav Nederländerna är den största givaren, och från privata stiftelser.

This contribution is a renewed phase of core support to the international organization International Centre for Transitional Justice (ICTJ) for a period of four years and with a total amount of 40 MSEK.
ICTJ is a key actor in the field of Transitional Justice (TJ), being both an expert organization, a policy development actor, and a partner to civil society, public institutions and governments at country level. ICTJ conducts long-term and comprehensive programs in a number of countries but also respond to requests for more ad hoc engagements in additional contexts when deemed relevant. ICTJ has its HQ in New York and offices in Brussels, The Hague, Colombia, Lebanon, Gambia, Tunisia and Uganda.
More specifically, the objectives of the intervention is that societies implement responsive, gender-sensitive and context-specific solutions to address legacies of massive human rights violations, and that practitioners and policymakers at the international level have better information and expanded capacity to advance such solutions. This will in turn contribute to prevent relapse into violent conflict and to build sustainable peace.
The total budget for ICTJ's operations for the four years is approximately 442 million SEK. Other contributions come from institutional donors, whereof the Netherlands is the main donor, and from private foundations.

sector.narrative: Civilian peace-building, conflict prevention and resolution

description.narrative:
Below are some examples of results from 2024/FY2025:
Syria: ICTJ created an opportunity for families of the missing and disappeared in Syria to share their needs and priorities directly with representatives of the transitional government. ICTJ leveraged its years of experience collaborating and building trust with the families of the disappeared to organize an unprecedented and historic meeting between the families and the government at the Presidential Palace in Damascus in February 2025. ICTJ worked closely with the families and the government in advance to ensure a structured, safe, and victim-centered conversation in which, for the first time, they were given space to voice their demands, concerns, and expectations for truth, justice and protection.
During the FY2025, ICTJ continued its close partnership with the Bridges of Truth, a coalition between ICTJ and seven Syrian civil society organizations based in Turkey and Lebanon dedicated to advocating for comprehensive justice for the victims of conflict and oppression in Syria. Together, they delivered an impactful international advocacy campaign to challenge repatriation narratives and reframe refugee return as a matter of justice and protection, not just logistics. ICTJ launched the report, The Accelerating Tragedy of Syrias Displaced, during a high-profile side event at the annual meeting of the ICCs Assembly of States Parties in The Hague.
Libanon/MENA: ICTJ strengthened Lebanese civil societies capacity to document past violations and enabled the National Commission for the Missing and Forcibly Disappeared (NCMFDL) to take concrete steps towards implementing its mandate to uncover the fate of the missing and disappeared. They achieved this impact by assisting the Committee of the Kidnapped and Disappeared in Lebanon (CFKDL) to produce a digital archive and website and by providing technical support to the National Commission for its operationalization.
Ukraine: In ICTJs efforts to support the development of a holistic, victim-centered, inclusive transitional justice strategy for Ukraine that complements legal accountability with truth-seeking, reparations and reintegration, ICTJ enhanced policymakers and civil society actors knowledge of comparative experiences on transitional justice and their applicability to the Ukrainian context. They achieved this by convening a series of five online dialogues in collaboration with Pathfinders for Peaceful, Just and Inclusive Societies at NYUs Center on International Cooperation. The series brought together representatives from the Ukrainian Government, experts with experience from other countries (particularly from the global south), donors, multilateral agencies, academia, and civil society to have a frank exchange of ideas on program and policy recommendations for victim-centered national and international justice responses to the ongoing war. Each dialogue covered a different topic: 1) MHPSS for victims of the conflict; 2) peoples daily justice needs during conflict; 3) victim-centered reparations for Ukraine; 4) bridging silos in emergency response; and 5) maintaining social cohesion to strengthen Ukraine's continued efforts to build a democratic and pluralistic society.
Regional Africa: During the second year of the Initiative for Transitional Justice in Africa (ITJA), led by ICTJ in partnership with the African Transitional Justice Legacy Fund and the Center for the Study of Violence and Reconciliation, interest in transitional justice continues to grow across the continent despite violent conflict and political instability persists. ICTJ and its ITJA Project partners helped to drive a marked shift in AU member states attitudes towards transitional justice from distrust and evasion to cautious engagement and normalization, exemplified by Ethiopias adoption of a National Transitional Justice Policy, The Gambias selection of commissioners for its Reparations Commission, and South Sudans passage of laws to establish a Commission on Truth, Reconciliation, and Healing (CTRH) and a Compensation and Reparations Authority (CRA), among others. This impact was achieved by providing technical expertise to African countries pursuing transitional justice processes, including Ethiopia, The Gambia, Lesotho, and IGAD; convening major policy events on transitional justice in Africa, including the AU-EU Expert Seminar and the African Transitional Justice Forum; advancing the production of knowledge on African transitional justice experiences; and supporting civil society organizations working on transitional justice throughout the continent.
Uganda: Sustained engagement with government stakeholders is often necessary for achieving a lasting impact, demonstrated through ICTJs five-year collaboration with the National Identification and Registration Authority in Uganda. Through continuous engagement, they have transformed the Authority's passive indifference to active ownership of the registration process for children born of war.
